decisions.question: Where should Ariviso live?
decisions.context: Settled: a separate private repository, ariakit/ariviso. D60 changes the earlier working name Visuaria to Ariviso; the original note is retained as history. Ariakit is its first client. Public npm packages do not make the application repository public.

options.label: Separate Ariviso monorepo
options.detail: Ariakit is the first client. Keep the app, protocol, importer, and capture adapter in Ariviso.

options.label: Inside Ariakit at first
options.detail: Use a private workspace and extract it later. Define package boundaries now to limit that move.

decisions.question: What does A or X change?
decisions.context: Settled: A/X changes the current variant. F shows only the new screenshot. Shift+A/X changes the whole item (D21).

options.label: Current variant; separate whole-item actions
options.detail: Each browser/theme result has its own verdict. Group status summarizes those verdicts.

options.label: Every changed variant in the item
options.detail: Fewer actions, but easier to accept a variant that has not been inspected.

decisions.notes: We should also have an option besides side by side and pixel diff that we activate with F and show the full new screenshot only (no old). By the way, what would be the shortcuts for the separate whole-item actions? Maybe Shift+A and Shift+X or Mod+A/Mod+X (Mod=Ctrl or Cmd)?

decisions.question: What should happen after approval or rejection?
decisions.context: Settled: after the server saves a verdict, move to the next pending variant. Proposed detail: wrap once through the visible review order; stay on the current variant when no pending variants remain.

options.label: Stay on this variant
options.detail: Use arrow keys when ready to move. Provide an optional personal auto-advance setting.

options.label: Go to the next pending variant
options.detail: Move within the item, then to the next item. Undo restores the previous location.

decisions.question: Which variant should open when up/down changes the item?
decisions.context: Settled: remember the last selected variant separately for each item. First visit starts at its first variant. Auto-advance selects the next pending variant and updates that item’s memory.

options.label: Keep the matching variant key
options.detail: If absent, choose the first variant and announce the fallback. Stop at navigation boundaries.

options.label: Always open the first variant
options.detail: Simple and predictable, but repeats theme/browser selection.

options.label: Remember the last variant for each item
options.detail: Good for return visits. The displayed condition can change as you move down the list.

decisions.question: Should React and Solid share one item?
decisions.context: The current capture names include the framework. Grouping frameworks reduces rows but increases variants per item.

options.label: Framework is a variant dimension
options.detail: One item for the same state across React and Solid. Keep explicit framework labels.

options.label: Separate React and Solid items
options.detail: Shorter variant lists and independent histories, but more rows for the same visual state.

decisions.question: How should the first adapter assign stable item keys?
decisions.context: Confirmed in follow-up: explicit stable keys, a fresh first batch, and no legacy import. All first-batch captures are new. Future key-renaming tools are separate work.

options.label: Explicit stable keys; fresh first batch
options.detail: Do not import old baselines or map legacy filenames. Capture the first full main batch as new items; the confirmed new-item rule accepts it automatically after validation.

options.label: Explicit stable keys with a legacy import map
options.detail: New and touched captures supply item and variant keys. Validate collisions in CI.

options.label: Derive keys from test titles at first
options.detail: Fastest migration. Renames create new history unless maintainers add a mapping.

decisions.notes:
We don't need a migration. It's fine if all screenshots are new in the first batch.
Confirmed: explicit keys, fresh first batch, no legacy import.

decisions.question: What makes a main-branch run the accepted baseline?
decisions.context: A complete main capture becomes the baseline when every change has valid acceptance. Eligible new items, new variants, and confirmed removals are accepted automatically. Existing-image changes and ineligible restoration or drift need review. Earlier acceptance counts only for exact eligible comparisons.

options.label: Full post-merge capture with valid review coverage
options.detail: Carry only eligible exact approvals. Hold promotion if merged output differs.

options.label: Any complete passing main capture
options.detail: Treat merge as acceptance. Main can absorb changes that were not reviewed in Ariviso.

options.label: Explicit maintainer promotion every time
options.detail: Strong control, but a separate action can delay all later comparisons.

decisions.notes: I'm not sure if this is what this option says, but the way I think about it is that when a PR diff is fully approved, once the PR is merged into main, that becomes the baseline. For commits that are made on main directly, if there are diffs, they should fail in CI and wait for approval in visuaria just as if it were a PR. Once the items are approved in visuaria for direct main commits, they are baseline. I also think we should consider that items approved from a PR right before it's merged might drift when they land on main (for example, due to a stale merged branch). In that case, those items that diff on main should be explicitly approved to become the baseline. Anyway, I think my explanation here became more complex than it should be. There should be a simple generic rule for this.

decisions.question: Can approval carry across retries, rebases, or merge queues?
decisions.context: Candidate image equality alone is insufficient. The reference, profile, comparison policy, and item/variant must also match.

options.label: Reuse only exact eligible comparison tuples
options.detail: Show the original reviewer or automatic policy and source run. Reuse only exact eligible acceptance. Changed tuples need review; first-introduction automatic acceptance is a separate rule.

options.label: Require a fresh review for every tested SHA
options.detail: Simpler policy and less reuse logic, but can require repeated approval of identical images.

decisions.question: Whose approval is enough to pass?
decisions.context: When explicit human approval is needed, one current maintainer is enough, including the PR author. Automatic acceptance records its policy as the source, not a fictional reviewer.

options.label: One maintainer, including the PR author
options.detail: Fits a small maintainer team. Record the actor and preserve the audit history.

options.label: One maintainer other than the PR author
options.detail: Adds independent review. Solo changes wait for another maintainer.

options.label: Two maintainers
options.detail: Stronger review coverage with more coordination and a more complex verdict model.

decisions.question: When should external fork pull requests get Ariviso runs?
decisions.context: Settled: maintainer branches first. The maintainer confirmed that Ariakit currently restricts PRs to collaborators. Fork capture and import are deferred.

options.label: Support forks in the first release
options.detail: Use unprivileged captures and trusted import. More integration work, useful for contributors.

options.label: Maintainer branches first
options.detail: Support collaborator branches in the first release. Add fork support only if repository policy later requires it.

decisions.notes: The repo has PRs restricted to collaborators only anyway.

decisions.question: Must old runs be recomparable without a new CI job?
decisions.context: Settled: the service compares stored captures independently of CI. Cloudflare Queues plus a separate comparison Worker is the proposed runtime; codec and resource probes remain required.

options.label: Compare in the trusted importer first
options.detail: Keep a pinned comparator in CI. Recomparison starts a trusted job using stored images.

options.label: Independent service comparison at launch
options.detail: Use a queue and a measured compute runtime. Add retries, resource controls, and derived-result state.

decisions.question: Can maintainers review before all captures arrive?
decisions.context: Early review needs provisional states and exact group scopes. Sealing first avoids new variants arriving after a whole-item action.

options.label: Only after the run is sealed
options.detail: Allow upload progress and errors immediately. Enable verdicts only after completeness checks.

options.label: Allow provisional review
options.detail: Approve exact arrived pairs, but never pass the run until all expected captures are sealed.

decisions.question: Who can view screenshots and review results?
decisions.context: The app, review results, reviewer names, and per-image verdicts stay private to current Ariakit maintainers. The maintainer explicitly allows public URLs for validated screenshot bytes. A copied image URL can be read without login.

options.label: Ariakit maintainers only
options.detail: Use private R2 delivery through the authenticated app.

options.label: Anyone can view; maintainers can decide
options.detail: Make publication deliberate. Public caching is possible, but all captures must be safe to disclose.

options.label: Private app and review data; public image URLs
options.detail: Keep R2 private internally. A public image route serves validated originals, thumbnails, and masks. It exposes no review metadata, manifests, or quarantine.

decisions.question: How does Ariviso determine who is a maintainer?
decisions.context: GitHub login does not imply repository permission. Organization membership alone is too broad.

options.label: Repository write permission or higher
options.detail: Follow existing repository access. Verify role semantics with the GitHub permission endpoint.

options.label: A named GitHub team
options.detail: A precise review group. Requires a team name and organization membership-read permission.

options.label: A fixed list of GitHub numeric user IDs
options.detail: Smallest policy implementation. Membership changes require configuration updates.

decisions.question: How long should closed-run images remain available?
decisions.context: Always keep active baselines, open reviews, and explicitly pinned evidence. These windows apply to unpinned closed runs.

options.label: 30 days
options.detail: Lowest retained volume. Older review pages retain metadata but cannot show expired images.

options.label: 90 days
options.detail: More time to investigate releases, with modest storage growth at the current size.

options.label: One year
options.detail: Longest easy history, with more cleanup and storage exposure.

decisions.question: Should launch storage deduplicate exact bytes across runs?
decisions.context: R2 is cheap at the measured scale. Deduplication lowers repeat writes, but safe deletion needs a shared-blob reference protocol.

options.label: Per-run objects first
options.detail: Copy promoted baseline bytes into a protected snapshot prefix. Use simple retention; add deduplication if measured cost warrants it.

options.label: Content-addressed shared objects at launch
options.detail: Skip repeated bytes and uploads. Prove cleanup, upload, and promotion races before enabling deletion.

decisions.question: Which default visual direction fits review work?
decisions.context: The prototype uses calm dark surfaces, a compact item list, and words plus color for state. Both options use copied Ariakit UI components.

options.label: Compact, mostly flat controls
options.detail: Keep more images and variants on screen. Keep touch targets large on coarse pointers.

options.label: More spacing and subtle bevels
options.detail: Easier scanning and stronger controls, with fewer items visible at once.

decisions.question: Which parts need published packages at launch?
decisions.context: Settled: publish the Playwright adapter and CLI from the private monorepo. Keep web/server code private. Package names and the supported-version matrix still need a release specification.

options.label: Private packages for the initial pilot
options.detail: Install Ariakit integration from a pinned workspace build or release artifact. Add public packages after the contract settles.

options.label: Publish the Playwright adapter and CLI
options.detail: Use Changesets and trusted publishing. Package names and supported versions become public contracts. npm provenance is unavailable from the private source repository.

decisions.question: Which branches must the first release support?
decisions.context: One baseline branch is easier to operate. Release branches require independent baseline selection and promotion.

options.label: Main plus PR and merge-queue runs targeting main
options.detail: Keep branch identity in the schema. Add release branch support later.

options.label: Main and supported release branches
options.detail: Treat each target as a separate baseline stream. Add backport and branch-fork tests.

decisions.question: When should Ariviso block merges?
decisions.context: Require Ariviso immediately after setup and readiness checks, with no optional pilot. Eligible new items, new variants, and confirmed removals can pass automatically. Unapproved existing changes, rejection, incomplete capture, and stale acceptance still block the required check.

options.label: Required after a short optional pilot
options.detail: Keep the check optional for a short trial after setup, then require it. New-item acceptance is a separate rule in either rollout.

options.label: Required immediately after setup
options.detail: Create the fresh baseline automatically, verify the stated readiness checks, and require Ariviso from the first supported PR. No optional pilot. Unapproved changes and service failures can stop a merge.

decisions.notes:
I still don't understand this. New items should be pre-approved. Isn't that the standard in the industry?
Confirmed: Require Visuaria immediately; automatically approve new items.

decisions.question: Which shortcuts should change the whole item?
decisions.context: Settled: Shift+A and Shift+X change the whole item. A/X changes the current variant. Keep Cmd/Ctrl+A for Select All and Cmd/Ctrl+X for Cut.

options.label: Shift+A / Shift+X
options.detail: Approve or reject all changed variants in the current sealed item as one undoable command.

options.label: Cmd/Ctrl+A / Cmd/Ctrl+X
options.detail: Use platform modifier keys, but override Select All and Cut while the review workspace has focus.

options.label: Buttons only for whole-item actions
options.detail: Keep A/X for the current variant. Whole-item decisions require the visible controls.

decisions.question: What should undo do after approval made main the baseline?
decisions.context: Settled: undo a saved approval and its promotion atomically if that promoted snapshot is still current. Refuse ordinary undo after a later promotion. Automatic acceptance does not invent a maintainer command in the session undo stack.

options.label: Undo the promotion if it is still current
options.detail: Atomically undo the verdict and restore the prior accepted snapshot. If a later snapshot has replaced it, refuse ordinary undo and offer an explicit recovery flow.

options.label: Require explicit recovery after promotion
options.detail: Ordinary undo ends when the approved main snapshot becomes the baseline. Preserve that snapshot and start a separate correction/recovery action.

decisions.question: Should a new variant of an existing item be approved automatically?
decisions.context: Settled: automatically approve a new variant of an existing item, including a newly added browser, theme, or framework. Apply the same validation and exact acceptance rules as for new items. Changes to a previously accepted variant still need review.

options.label: Automatically approve new variants too
options.detail: Adding Firefox or dark mode starts its history without a manual approval. Record that the service accepted it automatically.

options.label: Review new variants of existing items
options.detail: New items still pass automatically. A new condition inside an existing item waits for a maintainer.

decisions.question: How should rejection work after automatic acceptance promoted main?
decisions.context: Keep an automatically promoted baseline, including a confirmed removal under D59. Historical X makes no change and the automatic service action creates no Undo command. Correct it through a new complete main capture. Existing-image corrections need review; a restored identity follows D35 exact eligible reuse. D22 still governs saved human approval.

options.label: Reject and roll back if that promotion is current
options.detail: Use an explicit audited recovery action. Restore the previous snapshot (or the empty initial state), revoke this acceptance, and recompare affected active runs. If a later promotion exists, refuse rollback and explain recovery.

options.label: Keep the baseline; correct it in a new main capture
options.detail: Smallest recovery model. Do not allow historical rejection to alter the accepted snapshot. Fix the image in a new commit, review the resulting change, and move forward.

decisions.question: What may Ariviso show in Ariakit’s public GitHub checks?
decisions.context: Generic public GitHub status and a sign-in review link remain selected. Reviewer names and per-image results stay private. D13 now permits direct public image URLs, but does not add images to GitHub check output.

options.label: Generic status plus a sign-in review link
options.detail: Public readers see the result and can reach the login page. Only current maintainers can read the review.

options.label: Generic status only; open Ariviso separately
options.detail: Keep the same public status but omit the review link. Maintainers navigate to Ariviso themselves.

decisions.question: Can A/X edit a human-approved run after it promoted main?
decisions.context: Settled: any current maintainer can reject a human-approved variant and roll back its promotion while that promotion is still current, even after reload or without the original approval command. D22 Undo and D24 automatic-history protection remain separate.

options.label: History is read-only except eligible Undo
options.detail: A/X cannot change promoted history. Offer D22 Undo when eligible; otherwise correct the code in a new capture.

options.label: Allow X to reject and roll back the current promotion
options.detail: Any authorized maintainer can reject the current human-approved promotion through an audited rollback, even without the original Undo command. Later promotions still prevent rollback.

decisions.question: Who prepares each variant in the public capture API?
decisions.context: Settled: Ariakit prepares the page and calls the public adapter once per variant. The adapter captures that prepared condition; the reporter groups calls by stable item key. Theme, viewport, and page preparation remain in the Ariakit wrapper.

options.label: Ariakit prepares it; capture one variant per call
options.detail: The Ariakit wrapper owns theme, viewport, and page setup. Ariviso captures the prepared page and groups calls through its reporter. Smallest adapter.

options.label: Ariviso iterates variants with a preparation callback
options.detail: The adapter controls the loop and awaits a supplied preparation callback before each capture. Specify callback errors, cleanup, and ordering.

decisions.question: When the next-pending search reaches the end, should it wrap?
decisions.context: D03 already selects the next pending variant. This chooses what happens when earlier visible variants still need review. If none remain, stay and announce completion under either option.
decisions.scenario: You approve item 8. Item 2 is still pending; nothing after item 8 is pending.

options.label: Wrap once to the first pending variant
options.detail: Find remaining work in one pass through the visible order. The selection can move to an earlier item.
options.example: Selection moves from item 8 to item 2. Undo returns to item 8.

options.label: Stop at the end and offer a jump
options.detail: Keep forward navigation predictable. Show a button to reach earlier pending work.
options.example: Selection stays on item 8. Announce one pending item and show “Go to remaining review”.

decisions.question: Where should removed items appear in the review list?
decisions.context: The list must include candidate and reference-only identities. Existing thumbnail rules stay fixed: a retained item uses its first candidate variant; a wholly removed item uses its first reference variant.
decisions.scenario: Reference order is A, B, C. The new run contains C, A, D; B was removed.

options.label: Candidate order, then removed items
options.detail: Follow the new run order and append removed identities in their previous order. Smallest ordering rule.
options.example: List: C, A, D, B (Removed). B keeps its old first-variant thumbnail.

options.label: Reference order, then new items
options.detail: Keep familiar positions for existing items; append new identities in candidate order.
options.example: List: A, B (Removed), C, D (New). Reordering in the capture plan does not reorder existing rows yet.

decisions.question: What should D show for a new or removed image?
decisions.context: F shows the new image, or “Removed — no new image”. S shows the existing image next to a labeled empty pane. D has no ordinary before/after pair in these cases.
decisions.scenario: A 600 × 400 image was removed. The reviewer presses D.

options.label: Show a labeled full-image change mask
options.detail: Make the entire addition or removal visible. State that it is not a paired pixel comparison.
options.example: D shows a 600 × 400 red removal mask with “Removed — full image”. S still shows the original.

options.label: Make pixel diff unavailable for this case
options.detail: Avoid implying measured pair differences. Keep F and S available.
options.example: D shows “Pixel diff needs two images”. Offer S to inspect the removed original.

decisions.question: Should my Undo history survive a page reload?
decisions.context: D22/D26 revision checks and D24 automatic-history protection apply in both options. This chooses the lifetime of the personal command stack, not whether audit history survives.
decisions.scenario: You reject a current human-approved promotion, then reload the page.

options.label: Current review session only
options.detail: Keep the initial Undo stack in the current page. Audit history and D26 rejection remain available after reload.
options.example: The rejection remains recorded, but the page has no saved Undo stack. A new review action still follows all current revision checks.

options.label: Restore my eligible commands after reload
options.detail: Load your recent commands for this run from server history. Show conflicts and retain required evidence while Undo is offered.
options.example: Reload offers Undo for your rejection if no decision or baseline revision has intervened. Another reviewer’s command is never yours to undo.

decisions.question: How should one prepared capture be called from a Playwright test?
decisions.context: D27 keeps page preparation in Ariakit and one variant per capture call. The exact import, function shape, and metadata boundary are still proposed. Both options require explicit stable item and variant keys.
decisions.scenario: Ariakit has prepared the dark dialog in a test that already has a page fixture.

options.label: A page function with explicit variant metadata
options.detail: Propose visual(page, { item, name, variant: { key, ...dimensions } }). Works with existing page helpers; the reporter groups results.
options.example: await prepareDarkDialog(page); await visual(page, { item: "dialog/open", variant: { key: "react-chromium-dark", browser: "chromium", colorScheme: "dark" } });

options.label: A Playwright fixture with a capture method
options.detail: Propose ariviso.capture({ item, name, variant: { key, ...dimensions } }). The fixture supplies the page and observed browser metadata; Ariakit still prepares the state. Adds fixture integration.
options.example: await prepareDarkDialog(page); await ariviso.capture({ item: "dialog/open", variant: { key: "react-chromium-dark", colorScheme: "dark" } });

decisions.question: How should capture clients and the service evolve together?
decisions.context: Both paths validate manifests, reject duplicate keys, preserve explicit identities and deterministic ordering, and reject an unknown schema. The choice is the compatibility promise for public clients.
decisions.scenario: The service is updated while Ariakit still uses the previously published adapter.

options.label: Versioned manifest with compatible optional additions
options.detail: Use a schema major version. Within that major, retain documented old-client support and ignore only explicitly optional extensions. More compatibility fixtures.
options.example: An old supported client still uploads. A client using an unknown major receives an actionable version error.

options.label: Require matching protocol releases initially
options.detail: Publish an exact client/service protocol compatibility table and coordinate upgrades. Smaller initial compatibility surface; more upgrade coupling.
options.example: If the old protocol is no longer listed, the service refuses the upload and identifies the compatible client version.

decisions.question: Where is first automatic acceptance reserved for an unused key?
decisions.context: First automatic acceptance is scoped to a verified PR/main lineage. D07/D08 require exact eligible reuse and review of later drift. Independent PRs do not share introduction records; atomic creation on the active valid attempt remains required.
decisions.scenario: Two unrelated PRs introduce the same unused key: PR A captures blue; PR B captures green. Neither has reached main.

options.label: Per verified PR/main lineage
options.detail: Each independent introduction has its own first acceptance. Main still compares the actual merged result against its current baseline. An abandoned PR does not reserve the key globally.
options.example: Both first introductions can be accepted automatically in their own lineage. If A lands first, B’s later blue → green main comparison needs review.

options.label: Once across the project
options.detail: Reserve the first valid introduction project-wide. Other lineages need review unless D08 permits reuse. Reveals key collisions earlier, but abandoned PRs can add review work.
options.example: A reserves the first introduction. B’s green capture needs review; it cannot use A’s unrelated acceptance.

decisions.question: Should a removed identity need fresh approval when it returns?
decisions.context: The selected rule permits an earlier acceptance only when its full comparison tuple, profiles, policy, source revision, and verified lineage remain eligible under D08. A restored key alone is not new. Missing expected reference bytes remain an error. D59 separately accepts confirmed removals automatically. A correction that restores a removed identity follows this D35 rule.
decisions.scenario: An accepted removal deleted item K. A later run restores the same key and pixels.

options.label: Require fresh review after accepted removal
options.detail: Removal ends earlier introduction eligibility. The return stays visible even when it matches old pixels.
options.example: K appears as Restored and needs approval. Old automatic acceptance cannot approve this return.

options.label: Allow exact eligible earlier acceptance
options.detail: Permit reuse only when the earlier absent → image tuple, capture profiles, policy, and verified lineage all remain eligible. Adds restoration reuse rules.
options.example: If every D08 field and lineage matches, K can reuse its earlier acceptance. Otherwise it needs review. Matching pixels alone are insufficient.

decisions.notes: Should we automatically accept deleted items too? How's the industry standard?

decisions.question: May a later full main run pass an earlier pending run?
decisions.context: Both options preserve full snapshots, ancestry checks, exact acceptance, and refusal of stale promotions. This chooses scheduling when main receives another commit before review finishes.
decisions.scenario: Main run A changes gray to blue and is pending. Descendant run B captures green.

options.label: Yes, after a complete comparison
options.detail: Compare B against the current accepted baseline and resolve every remaining inherited change. Reverted changes can disappear. Prevent A from overwriting B later.
options.example: B can promote after gray → green has valid acceptance. A remains historical and cannot move the baseline backward.

options.label: Resolve or supersede earlier runs first
options.detail: Process main captures in commit order. Easier chronology, but obsolete changes can hold up a later baseline.
options.example: B waits until A is accepted or explicitly superseded. Then compare B with the resulting current baseline.

decisions.question: Should launch accept intentionally partial capture runs?
decisions.context: Only a full trusted run can infer removals, promote main, or satisfy the required check. This chooses whether informational subset runs exist at launch.
decisions.scenario: A maintainer captures only one dialog test to inspect a change.

options.label: Accept full runs only at launch
options.detail: Keep the first public run protocol small. Focused captures remain local until subset support is added.
options.example: Ariviso refuses the subset as an unsupported run type and asks for the full capture plan.

options.label: Support informational subset runs
options.detail: Allow focused review with clear coverage labels and a separate result. Never let it substitute for the required full run.
options.example: Ariviso shows the one test as an informational subset. Missing items are not removals; the merge check still waits for a full run.

decisions.question: How should failed-job-only workflow reruns work?
decisions.context: GitHub test retries and workflow reruns are different. A new workflow attempt must have complete trusted coverage before it can pass; incompatible shards cannot be combined.
decisions.scenario: Chromium and Firefox passed. Only the failed WebKit job is rerun at the same tested commit.

options.label: Require Re-run all jobs
options.detail: Leave the partial new attempt incomplete and give a clear recovery instruction. Avoid shard inheritance at launch.
options.example: WebKit alone cannot seal the new attempt. The reviewer sees “Re-run all jobs to produce a complete capture”.

options.label: Inherit verified successful shards
options.detail: Reuse non-rerun shards only at the same tested SHA and plan/profile identities. Record each source attempt and prove supersession rules. Saves CI work.
options.example: The service verifies the old Chromium/Firefox shards, combines them with the successful new WebKit shard, then validates the complete run.

decisions.question: Where should the authoritative capture plan live?
decisions.context: The plan defines the full suite invocation and required jobs. A PR manifest cannot prove its own completeness or relax its gate. Changes to trusted plan configuration need a deliberate rollout in both options.
decisions.scenario: A PR reports coverage: "full" but leaves out the Firefox job.

options.label: Ariakit’s trusted main configuration
options.detail: Read and pin an approved configuration revision for each run. Keep suite and matrix maintenance with the capture project.
options.example: The pinned main plan requires Firefox. The run stays incomplete despite the PR manifest’s claim.

options.label: Ariviso service configuration
options.detail: Keep the allowed invocation and matrix in service configuration. Strong separation from PR files; matrix changes require coordinated service updates.
options.example: The service-owned plan requires Firefox. The run stays incomplete; a plan change must be made in Ariviso configuration.

decisions.question: Which private capture upload path should launch use?
decisions.context: Uploads enter private quarantine. D13 permits validated image URLs to be public; manifests, diagnostics, and review data stay private. Upload capabilities cannot read private data, approve, or promote. Bind ingest to verified repository, workflow, run, attempt, and tested commit.
decisions.scenario: A collaborator capture job must submit screenshots and private capture metadata to Ariviso.

options.label: GitHub OIDC and short-lived capabilities
options.detail: Verify the job identity and issue bounded upload capabilities. No long-lived upload secret in CI. Requires OIDC integration tests.
options.example: The verified job receives a short-lived upload capability. Reusing it for another run or a review action is refused.

options.label: A scoped Infisical upload credential
options.detail: Start with a stored upload-only credential, explicit rotation, and the same trusted run validation. Smaller identity integration, more secret handling.
options.example: The job authenticates with its scoped credential. The service still verifies the run and issues bounded upload tickets.

options.label: Encrypted GitHub artifact transport
options.detail: Keep artifact transport but encrypt private content for verified GitHub App import. Adds key rotation, authenticated envelopes, and archive validation. Cleartext artifacts remain forbidden.
options.example: GitHub stores ciphertext. Trusted ingest validates and decrypts it privately; the public artifact never reveals screenshots.

decisions.question: How should image bytes reach private quarantine?
decisions.context: This applies to direct uploads after authorization. Encrypted artifact transport uses the import path instead. Both options hash and validate bytes on the trusted side before they become eligible.
decisions.scenario: A capture job uploads a batch containing its largest supported screenshot.

options.label: Bounded upload through the Worker
options.detail: One route enforces ticket scope and body limits. Measure the largest supported upload before launch.
options.example: The Worker checks the ticket and byte limit, writes quarantine, and schedules validation. Oversized or mismatched content is refused.

options.label: Short-lived presigned R2 upload
options.detail: Send bytes directly to R2. Requires expiration, CORS, bearer-URL protection, and trusted validation after upload.
options.example: The client PUTs to a temporary R2 URL. The object remains quarantined until trusted hashing and image validation pass.

decisions.question: Which image and color contract should launch accept?
decisions.context: Ariakit already captures lossless WebP through Playwright 1.63. The follow-up selects both lossless WebP and PNG originals. Preserve their bytes and test both decoders against a defined sRGB and alpha contract; unknown profiles fail clearly. No legacy import is needed.
decisions.scenario: One capture is plain sRGB PNG. Another has an embedded color profile; a third is lossless WebP.

options.label: Static 8-bit sRGB PNG only
options.detail: Start with one format and a precisely supported color contract. Validate signature, chunks, CRC, depth, animation, and allowed color metadata. Reject unsupported profiles.
options.example: The supported PNG enters comparison. Unsupported profile data and WebP receive clear format errors; neither is silently normalized.

options.label: PNG with tested color normalization
options.detail: Still use PNG originals, but normalize supported profiles to a defined comparison space. More color fixtures and codec work.
options.example: The profiled PNG is compared only after verified normalization. WebP remains unsupported. Unknown profiles still fail.

options.label: Lossless WebP and PNG
options.detail: Accept both lossless formats. Preserve captured originals, validate each format and supported color data, and test equivalent decoded pixels. This does not require Ariakit to switch to PNG.
options.example: Both supported formats can enter comparison. Unsupported profiles fail; byte savings and decoded equivalence remain pending measurements.

options.label: Lossless WebP only
options.detail: Keep one source format and decoder. Fits current Ariakit capture, but excludes PNG clients.
options.example: The lossless WebP enters comparison under the tested color contract. PNG gets a clear unsupported-format error.

decisions.notes: I don't understand this question. Aren't we using webp?

decisions.question: Which pixel-difference policy should launch use?
decisions.context: The existing helper uses threshold 0 and maxDiffPixelRatio 0.0005; full-page tolerance is zero. Effective policy comes from trusted configuration, and changes invalidate incompatible acceptance.
decisions.scenario: A 1,000,000-pixel normal capture changes 100 pixels. A full-page capture changes one pixel.

options.label: Retain and prove Ariakit’s current policy
options.detail: Pin the comparison engine and test thresholds, antialias behavior, alpha, and dimensions against the current helper. Preserve full-page strictness.
options.example: Subject to proved engine parity, the normal capture is within the 0.0005 ratio; the full-page capture needs review. This model does not prove comparator parity.

options.label: Require zero changed pixels everywhere
options.detail: Use a simple strict rule for every capture. It can create more review work for harmless rendering noise.
options.example: Both captures need review. Any decoded-pixel difference is a change.

options.label: Select a new policy from a defect/noise study
options.detail: Benchmark known defects and stable repeats, then return with explicit proposed thresholds before launch. No implicit perceptual or AI approval.
options.example: The policy remains unchosen until the study has results and the exact threshold proposal is accepted. No run passes under guessed tolerances.

decisions.question: How should the adapter confirm stable pixels?
decisions.context: D27 keeps theme and page preparation in Ariakit. Stability is a separate bounded capture check. A timeout fails the capture, including new items; stable dimensions alone cannot pass.
decisions.scenario: A prepared dialog has fixed dimensions, but its pixels continue to change.

options.label: Adapter preserves current assertion stability
options.detail: Reproduce the current helper’s observed consecutive-capture behavior with equivalent options. Pin deadlines from the validated capture configuration.
options.example: The adapter retries before upload and fails if the required stable result is not reached. Exact parity with today’s assertion remains a fixture test.

options.label: Adapter requires an exact repeated image
options.detail: Require two consecutive captures with identical decoded pixels within a configured deadline. Clearer rule, potentially stricter than existing behavior.
options.example: No identical consecutive pair appears, so the adapter fails the capture. No automatic acceptance is created.

decisions.question: What if the comparison Worker fails codec or resource tests?
decisions.context: D11 already requires independent service comparison. Keep originals, deterministic results, bounded retries, and the queue contract under every runtime option. No runtime probe has passed yet.
decisions.scenario: The largest supported image pair exceeds the Worker’s measured safe memory use.

options.label: Worker first; test a Container fallback
options.detail: Validate the simpler Worker path first. If it fails, test a pinned native decoder in a Container behind the same queue contract before launch.
options.example: The Worker path is rejected for this workload. A Container is eligible only after its codec, resource, cost, and retry evidence passes.

options.label: Worker only for launch
options.detail: Block launch until the agreed supported captures fit and compare correctly. Do not silently reduce the supported image limits.
options.example: Launch stays blocked. Optimize or return with an explicit capture-limit change; no CI-comparison fallback is introduced.

options.label: Container first
options.detail: Start with a pinned native decoder and accept the additional lifecycle and cost work. Still measure the full supported workload.
options.example: The Container is the first runtime tested. A failed Container probe still blocks readiness.

decisions.question: How long may image-read permission be cached?
decisions.context: Recorded selection: up to five minutes for protected image reads. The later public-image clarification makes this policy inactive for launch image delivery. Public images have no image-read permission check. This answer does not create a five-minute cache policy for private app metadata; protected app routes retain current permission checks.
decisions.scenario: A maintainer loses write permission just after a successful image-read authorization check.

options.label: Up to five minutes for reads
options.detail: Reduce GitHub API requests. Accept a bounded read-revocation delay; invalidate on relevant membership events and fail closed after expiry.
options.example: Inactive for launch public image URLs. If protected image reads were reintroduced: A cached read may continue for at most five minutes. Review writes recheck access and are refused once revocation is observed.

options.label: Check every protected read
options.detail: Reduce cache-based revocation delay. Increase latency and dependency on GitHub API availability.
options.example: Inactive for launch public image URLs. If protected image reads were reintroduced: The next protected read checks GitHub. A denied or unavailable authorization result does not return image data.

decisions.notes: If I understand correctly, we will be limiting image read directly on R2? Is it complex? I mean, I just wanted the app to stay private to maintainers, but I don't mind if the images can be directly accessed. Is this an issue?
decisions.applicability: Inactive under D13 public image URLs. Do not apply this image-read choice to private app metadata.

decisions.question: Which image storage and delivery path should launch use?
decisions.context: The maintainer retained private R2 Standard storage and clarified that image URLs may be public. Keep exact per-run originals and 30-day unpinned closed-run retention. The app and review data remain private.
decisions.scenario: A signed-out person has a copied image URL and a link to its review page.

options.label: Private R2 Standard and authenticated Worker delivery
options.detail: Keep exact originals and generate small derived images. Use private browser caching initially. Smallest fidelity and access boundary in this design.
options.example: Every image route authorizes the viewer. Baseline bytes come from R2; no public bucket or shared cache bypass is used.

options.label: R2 originals with managed derived-image delivery
options.detail: Keep originals in R2 but evaluate managed thumbnail/mask delivery. Require proved private access and a measured transform/delivery cost before adoption.
options.example: Originals remain exact and private. Derived delivery stays unverified until direct URLs, cache behavior, revocation, and cost pass the selected tests.

options.label: Private R2 Standard with public Worker image URLs
options.detail: Expose validated image records through a read-only Worker route. The bucket, quarantine, manifests, and app metadata remain private. Public image requests do not need a maintainer cookie.
options.example: The copied URL serves the validated image. The review page still requires maintainer login. An arbitrary object key, quarantine file, or manifest is never served.

decisions.question: What if Better Auth with D1 fails deployed validation?
decisions.context: The requested GitHub-only Better Auth stack stays fixed. Current evidence is documentation and issue research, not a working deployment. This choice defines the failure response.
decisions.scenario: A pinned preview passes login but fails session renewal or concurrent requests.

options.label: Keep D1 and block launch until a supported setup passes
options.detail: Test minimal configuration, documented adapter changes, and verified fixes. Avoid undocumented workarounds.
options.example: Readiness stays failed. Re-run the auth suite after a supported fix; do not launch with broken sessions.

options.label: Prepare a separate auth-storage proposal
options.detail: Keep Better Auth and GitHub login, but return with a tested storage/service alternative, cost, and migration impact for a new decision.
options.example: The failed probe produces a new proposal. No replacement database or service is adopted automatically.

decisions.question: What names should the public adapter and CLI use?
decisions.context: D60 and the D61 follow-up replace the original naming targets: ariviso is the only CLI package, and @ariviso/playwright is the adapter. The selected repository is ariakit/ariviso. Historical naming options and the original note remain below. Registry control must still be proved before release.
decisions.scenario: Ariakit adds the adapter as a development dependency and invokes the CLI.

options.label: @ariakit/visuaria-playwright and @ariakit/visuaria-cli
options.detail: Keep ownership in the existing Ariakit namespace. Use visuaria as the proposed command name. This choice does not publish or reserve packages.
options.example: Example target: pnpm add -D @ariakit/visuaria-playwright @ariakit/visuaria-cli. Package availability is still unverified.

options.label: @visuaria/playwright and @visuaria/cli
options.detail: Give Visuaria its own npm namespace. Verify that maintainers can obtain and administer that scope.
options.example: Former working-name target, not selected: pnpm add -D @visuaria/playwright @visuaria/cli. The old registry lookups remain research evidence. D60/D61 now select ariviso and @ariviso/playwright.

options.label: ariviso CLI and @ariviso/playwright adapter
options.detail: Use the chosen Ariviso name. Publish the functional bare CLI with scoped library packages; no @ariviso/cli.
options.example:
pnpm add -D ariviso @ariviso/playwright
pnpm exec ariviso status
These are package targets, not published packages.

decisions.notes: We should also register "visuaria" just in case. But I also want to discuss the name. Is visuaria a good name? Can you suggest better alternatives? It's important that good domain TLDs, npm package names, and npm namespaces are available. For example, I thought about visionaria, which has the visionaria.dev domain available (does "vision" + "aria" make sense for a visual regression tool like this?). But it would be awesome if we could come up with a name that has a .com available. I don't know. Suggest a bunch of options after checking their availability.

decisions.question: Which toolchain must the first public release support?
decisions.context: D18 leaves the supported-version matrix open. Choose the scope, then record exact tested versions before publication. Capture browsers are distinct from the browsers used to review images.
decisions.scenario: A client reports a failure on a Node or Playwright version that Ariakit does not use.

options.label: Ariakit’s pinned toolchain first
options.detail: Test exact release-time Node, pnpm, and Playwright versions with Ariakit’s Linux and macOS capture jobs. Publish an explicit support table; expand through tested releases.
options.example: The release report lists the supported versions. An unlisted combination has no compatibility promise yet.

options.label: A broader tested client matrix at launch
options.detail: Cover declared active Node LTS lines and Playwright ranges across Linux, macOS, and Windows. More release tests and maintenance.
options.example: Every promised combination needs clean install, capture, upload, and error-path evidence before publication.

decisions.question: Which operations should the public CLI expose at launch?
decisions.context: In both options, a successful upload means complete data was accepted, not that visual review passed. Capture/upload errors return nonzero; status supports text and JSON. Capture CI does not wait for human approval. Exact flags and exit-code tables must follow the selected scope.
decisions.scenario: Upload finishes while a changed variant still needs approval; later a maintainer wants to recompare stored images.

options.label: Upload, finalize, and status only
options.detail: Keep the initial public contract small. Use the signed-in app for review, recompare, and export.
options.example: Upload returns success and a review URL. Status reports needs-review. Recomparison is requested in the app.

options.label: Also expose recompare and export
options.detail: Add authenticated maintenance commands with explicit permissions. Upload-only CI credentials cannot read images or request these operations.
options.example: Upload still returns before review. A separately authenticated maintainer can use proposed ariviso recompare and ariviso export commands.

decisions.question: What evidence must pass before the required check launches?
decisions.context: D20 remains required immediately after setup, with no optional pilot. This question defines setup evidence. Both choices require the client combinations selected in D50, review paths selected in D53, and limits required by D54 to pass. Staging covers only expansion beyond those contracts. Selecting a plan does not mark any production test passed or authorize implementation.
decisions.scenario: Core state tests pass, but the deployed accessibility and representative workload reports are missing.

options.label: Complete the full readiness set
options.detail: Require deployed evidence for protocol, capture/comparison, state conflicts, auth, GitHub integration, declared browser/accessibility scope, performance, and combined restore. Include a full Ariakit capture cycle.
options.example: Launch remains blocked until every required evidence row has a dated passing report. The local prototype is not a substitute.

options.label: Core correctness and recovery, with staged expansion
options.detail: Require privacy, auth, data integrity, baseline correctness, GitHub behavior, declared basic review support, and restore before launch. Defer only broader support/performance expansion, with no unsupported claims.
options.example: The declared core release can proceed only after its evidence passes. Untested expansion stays unavailable or explicitly unsupported; D20 still applies at first production use.

decisions.question: Which review-browser and accessibility paths must pass at launch?
decisions.context: Selected launch review support: Chrome Desktop and keyboard-only operation. Verify shortcuts and exclusions, focus, readable states, and zoom. Other review browsers, mobile workflows, and screen-reader certification are deferred. The screenshot capture browser matrix is unchanged.
decisions.scenario: A maintainer reviews with a keyboard in Chrome Desktop. Another asks whether Safari with VoiceOver or phone review is certified.

options.label: Chrome Desktop and keyboard-only review
options.detail: Verify Chrome Desktop, every keyboard action and exclusion, focus, readable states, and zoom. Defer other review browsers, mobile workflows, and screen-reader certification. Capture browser coverage stays unchanged.
options.example: Chrome Desktop keyboard review must pass. Safari, Firefox review, phone workflows, and screen-reader certification remain deferred; no claim is made from this prototype.

options.label: Desktop browsers and two screen-reader paths
options.detail: Verify current Chrome, Firefox, Safari, keyboard-only use, 200% text zoom, Windows forced colors, VoiceOver/Safari, and NVDA/Chrome or Firefox. Include real touch checks without a full mobile-workflow promise.
options.example: The desktop and assistive-technology paths need real results. A narrow prototype screenshot alone does not establish support.

options.label: Desktop and complete mobile review coverage
options.detail: Add iOS Safari and Android Chrome, orientation changes, touch navigation/zoom, and their screen-reader paths to the launch report. More device testing.
options.example: Both desktop and mobile workflows must pass before their support is claimed. Failures remain visible in the evidence ledger.

decisions.notes: This will be used internally at first so we only need Chrome Desktop for now and keyboard-only use.

decisions.question: How should performance and cost limits be chosen?
decisions.context: The account already has Workers Paid and may have other R2 use. Plan about ten times the current image count, with a lower but unmeasured mean size after splitting composite captures. Measure bytes, object operations, CPU, review latency, pins, backups, and shared-account incremental cost. Numeric limits remain a later decision.
decisions.scenario: The suite grows from 1,058 to about 10,580 captures per full run. Mean bytes shrink by an unknown amount; the account already uses Workers Paid and possibly R2.

options.label: Measure first, then approve numeric limits
options.detail: Benchmark the real suite, largest capture, and large review lists. Return with numeric limits and a full cost report before readiness is declared.
options.example: The benchmark yields evidence, not an automatic pass. The cost/latency/size limits remain open until the measured proposal is accepted.

options.label: Use draft planning targets now
options.detail: Propose Cloudflare at $25/month, full-suite comparison within 5 minutes, selected-image display within 2 seconds, cached navigation within 100 ms. Validate p95 timing on declared devices/network; list CI, domain, and secrets costs separately.
options.example: The selected targets are design budgets, not observed results. Measurements must meet them or trigger an explicit change; spending alerts do not authorize false check success.

decisions.notes: My account already has Workers Paid, and I think I'm already using R2 for another project. Also, keep in mind that the number of snapshots in the repo will increase a lot, probably 10x more what we have today, but the sizes might also decrease since right now we have a bunch of ariakit-ui sandbox snapshots that consist of several examples in single images. I did this to reduce the image bloat in the repo and reviews, but the idea with Visuaria is to separate them (plus we will have more examples and sandboxes).

decisions.question: What recovery plan should launch provide?
decisions.context: Back up database records and all original images needed for accepted baselines and retained reviews. Test both together. Apply current access and expiry rules after restore. D15 normal-run retention stays unchanged; backup copies have their own stated lifetime.
decisions.scenario: The live database and image storage are lost after a day of reviews.

options.label: Daily combined backup and tested manual restore
options.detail: Propose at most 24 hours of recent work at risk and restore within one working day. Keep 30 days of backup sets separate from live deletion. Prove the targets before launch.
options.example: Restore the latest complete database/image set, reapply current permissions and expiry, then reconcile checks. Work after that backup may be lost.

options.label: On-demand export and tested restore
options.detail: Export before destructive maintenance and before removing Git screenshots. Smaller operation burden, but potentially more lost recent work. Keep a protected last-known complete export.
options.example: Restore the last complete export. All later review work can be lost; the document must show its timestamp.

options.label: More frequent metadata and promotion checkpoints
options.detail: Propose hourly metadata recovery points plus image checkpoints after promotion. More coordination and storage; prove consistency and cost.
options.example: Restore the newest verified consistent checkpoint. An image-only or database-only checkpoint cannot be used as a complete recovery set.

decisions.question: How should stalled service work reach a maintainer?
decisions.context: Bounded retries, reconciliation, visible failure, and safe manual recovery are required in both options. A service outage never reports success. Select numeric deadlines from validated workloads. This design does not send or authorize messages.
decisions.scenario: A comparison exhausts retries and remains in the dead-letter queue.

options.label: Automatic recovery, then an actionable alert
options.detail: Alert a configured maintainer destination when work exceeds its agreed deadline or stays dead-lettered. Provide safe retry and restore instructions. Destination setup is later work.
options.example: The run remains failed or incomplete. The planned alert identifies the run and recovery action without leaking private images.

options.label: Dashboard-only escalation at launch
options.detail: Use the same automatic recovery, but maintainers find stalled work through the app and generic GitHub result. Avoid an outbound alert integration initially.
options.example: The dashboard shows the blocked run and a safe retry action. No outbound notification is planned.

decisions.question: Where should end-to-end GitHub behavior be proved before cutover?
decisions.context: D20 rejects an optional production pilot. These are pre-launch tests while Ariakit’s existing required visual workflow remains in place. Separate authorization is still needed to create repositories, deploy, or write checks.
decisions.scenario: The team must verify merge-group SHAs, stale success after rollback, missing shards, and full main promotion.

options.label: Disposable repository, then separate Ariakit diagnostics
options.detail: Exercise destructive/race scenarios in an isolated test project, then verify a real full Ariakit capture using a separate non-production diagnostic result before cutover.
options.example: Both reports are required. The existing required workflow remains active until the new service passes setup and becomes required.

options.label: Disposable test repository first
options.detail: Use realistic fixtures and a full Ariakit capture payload in isolation. Validate actual Ariakit integration during the controlled cutover setup. Less pre-cutover repo wiring.
options.example: The isolated report proves scenarios, while actual repository permissions and workflow wiring still require a cutover setup check.

options.label: Separate diagnostic runs on Ariakit
options.detail: Test real workflow wiring before cutover, using isolated Ariviso data and a distinct diagnostic check. Keep fault injection away from production state.
options.example: The old required workflow still governs merges. Diagnostic checks cannot approve real Ariviso baselines or replace the production requirement.

decisions.question: Can a recovered Playwright retry produce an eligible capture?
decisions.context: This is a retry of one test inside a workflow attempt, not D38’s job rerun. Exhausted retries and missing required captures fail in both options. Earlier failed-attempt images remain private diagnostics.
decisions.scenario: A test captures blue, fails later, retries, captures green, and passes.

options.label: Use the final successful test attempt
options.detail: Preserve Ariakit’s existing retry behavior. Select its captures before sealing and compare normally; retry success is not visual approval.
options.example: Only green enters the sealed capture set. Blue cannot establish acceptance. Green still needs normal validation and comparison.

options.label: Any test retry fails the visual capture run
options.detail: Make recovered flakiness block visual readiness. Stricter evidence at the cost of more CI failures.
options.example: The run fails because the test needed a retry, even though the last attempt passed. Neither blue nor green can pass this run.

decisions.question: Should confirmed removals be accepted automatically?
decisions.context: A complete trusted run automatically accepts a confirmed item or variant removal. Missing, failed, corrupt, or unavailable required captures remain errors. Keep a visible removal row, exact acceptance history, and the existing rejection and reuse guards. D24 protects automatically promoted removals; D35 controls a later restoration.
decisions.scenario: The baseline has button/light and button/dark. Case A: the new full trusted plan contains only button/light, and every planned capture succeeds. Case B: the plan still requires both variants, but button/dark never arrives.

options.label: Automatically accept confirmed removals
options.detail: Accept a confirmed removal after the full trusted run validates it. Keep its removal row and automatic-acceptance audit entry. Actual main capture, exact eligible reuse, and explicit rejection guards still apply. After automatic promotion, correct it in a new main capture; the service action creates no Undo command.
options.example: Case A: button/dark is shown as Removed and automatically accepted. Case B: the run fails as incomplete; button/dark is not accepted as removed. Restoring an accepted removal follows D35, not the new-item shortcut.

options.label: Keep manual approval for removals
options.detail: Alternative: a maintainer approves each confirmed removal or uses the whole-item action. This adds an explicit check for loss of visual coverage. Existing human-approval undo and current-promotion rollback rules apply.
options.example: Case A: button/dark is shown as Removed and stays pending until a maintainer approves it. Case B: the run fails as incomplete and cannot be approved as a valid removal.

decisions.question: Which project name should replace the current naming targets, if any?
decisions.context: Selected name: Ariviso. The private repository target is ariakit/ariviso. D61’s explicit follow-up selects ariviso as the only CLI package and @ariviso/playwright as the adapter. No domain, repository, package, or namespace has been created. Registry evidence remains provisional.
decisions.scenario: You choose the public project name before repository setup, domain registration, and package publication.

options.label: Visuaria (former working name)
options.detail: Return to the former visual + aria name. Its .com is registered, and graphic-design businesses use the name. The .dev remains a researched candidate. Package and namespace control would need validation.
options.example: Alternative targets: private ariakit/visuaria; visuaria for the CLI; @visuaria/playwright for the adapter; visuaria.dev as the domain candidate. Example: pnpm add -D visuaria @visuaria/playwright. No scoped CLI alias. This preview does not register or publish anything.

options.label: Ariviso
options.detail: Prefer a short Ariakit-linked name with no .com registration record. The visual meaning is less explicit than Snapvero. Package and namespace control still require validation.
options.example: Selected targets: private ariakit/ariviso; ariviso for the CLI; @ariviso/playwright for the adapter; ariviso.com as the domain candidate. Example: pnpm add -D ariviso @ariviso/playwright. No scoped CLI alias. This preview does not register or publish anything.

options.label: Snapvero
options.detail: Prefer a clear snapshot and verification cue with no .com registration record. The name has less connection to Ariakit. Package and namespace control still require validation.
options.example: Alternative targets: private ariakit/snapvero; snapvero for the CLI; @snapvero/playwright for the adapter; snapvero.com as the domain candidate. Example: pnpm add -D snapvero @snapvero/playwright. No scoped CLI alias. This preview does not register or publish anything.

options.label: Miravaria
options.detail: Emphasize looking at variants. The .com has no registration record, but the name is longer to say and type. Package and namespace control still require validation.
options.example: Alternative targets: private ariakit/miravaria; miravaria for the CLI; @miravaria/playwright for the adapter; miravaria.com as the domain candidate. Example: pnpm add -D miravaria @miravaria/playwright. No scoped CLI alias. This preview does not register or publish anything.

options.label: Snapluma
options.detail: Prefer a friendly visual name with no .com registration record. The name does not directly convey regression testing. Package and namespace control still require validation.
options.example: Alternative targets: private ariakit/snapluma; snapluma for the CLI; @snapluma/playwright for the adapter; snapluma.com as the domain candidate. Example: pnpm add -D snapluma @snapluma/playwright. No scoped CLI alias. This preview does not register or publish anything.

decisions.question: What should the bare project-name package provide?
decisions.context: Confirmed in follow-up: ariviso is the only CLI package. Use @ariviso/* for other packages, starting with @ariviso/playwright. Do not publish @ariviso/cli. This is a functional package choice, not an empty name reservation; publication is outside this design task.
decisions.scenario: Ariakit installs the CLI and adapter, then requests a run status.

options.label: ariviso as the only CLI package
options.detail: Publish a functional ariviso CLI and use @ariviso/playwright for the adapter. Other public libraries can use @ariviso/*; no @ariviso/cli alias.
options.example:
pnpm add -D ariviso @ariviso/playwright
pnpm exec ariviso status
Only ariviso publishes the CLI; @ariviso/playwright provides the capture adapter.

options.label: Bare CLI plus a scoped CLI alias
options.detail: Alternative, not selected: publish ariviso and @ariviso/cli for the same CLI. This creates an extra versioned package to maintain.
options.example: Alternative: pnpm add -D ariviso @ariviso/cli. Both expose the same CLI; release and support must keep them aligned.

options.label: Use only the two scoped packages
options.detail: Alternative, not selected: publish @ariviso/playwright and @ariviso/cli, with no bare ariviso package.
options.example: Alternative: install @ariviso/cli and use its ariviso binary. The bare package is not published.

decisions.notes: Let's do ariviso for the CLI (and use @ariviso/\* for other packages like playwright).

D02.notes: We should also have an option besides side by side and pixel diff that we activate with F and show the full new screenshot only (no old). By the way, what would be the shortcuts for the separate whole-item actions? Maybe Shift+A and Shift+X or Mod+A/Mod+X (Mod=Ctrl or Cmd)?

D06.notes:
We don't need a migration. It's fine if all screenshots are new in the first batch.
Confirmed: explicit keys, fresh first batch, no legacy import.

D07.notes: I'm not sure if this is what this option says, but the way I think about it is that when a PR diff is fully approved, once the PR is merged into main, that becomes the baseline. For commits that are made on main directly, if there are diffs, they should fail in CI and wait for approval in visuaria just as if it were a PR. Once the items are approved in visuaria for direct main commits, they are baseline. I also think we should consider that items approved from a PR right before it's merged might drift when they land on main (for example, due to a stale merged branch). In that case, those items that diff on main should be explicitly approved to become the baseline. Anyway, I think my explanation here became more complex than it should be. There should be a simple generic rule for this.

D10.notes: The repo has PRs restricted to collaborators only anyway.

D20.notes:
I still don't understand this. New items should be pre-approved. Isn't that the standard in the industry?
Confirmed: Require Visuaria immediately; automatically approve new items.

D35.notes: Should we automatically accept deleted items too? How's the industry standard?

D42.notes: I don't understand this question. Aren't we using webp?

D46.notes: If I understand correctly, we will be limiting image read directly on R2? Is it complex? I mean, I just wanted the app to stay private to maintainers, but I don't mind if the images can be directly accessed. Is this an issue?

D49.notes: We should also register "visuaria" just in case. But I also want to discuss the name. Is visuaria a good name? Can you suggest better alternatives? It's important that good domain TLDs, npm package names, and npm namespaces are available. For example, I thought about visionaria, which has the visionaria.dev domain available (does "vision" + "aria" make sense for a visual regression tool like this?). But it would be awesome if we could come up with a name that has a .com available. I don't know. Suggest a bunch of options after checking their availability.

D53.notes: This will be used internally at first so we only need Chrome Desktop for now and keyboard-only use.

D54.notes: My account already has Workers Paid, and I think I'm already using R2 for another project. Also, keep in mind that the number of snapshots in the repo will increase a lot, probably 10x more what we have today, but the sizes might also decrease since right now we have a bunch of ariakit-ui sandbox snapshots that consist of several examples in single images. I did this to reduce the image bloat in the repo and reviews, but the idea with Visuaria is to separate them (plus we will have more examples and sandboxes).

D61.notes: Let's do ariviso for the CLI (and use @ariviso/\* for other packages like playwright).

newItems.source: D20 note and explicit follow-up: Require Visuaria immediately; automatically approve new items.
newItems.scope: Eligible new items, including the first project batch. D23 covers new variants; D59 separately covers confirmed removals. Existing-image changes and ineligible restoration or drift still require valid review.

newVariants.scope: First valid introduction of a new variant of an existing item. Existing approval reuse and drift rules remain unchanged.

automaticBaselineCorrection.scope: Keep the automatically promoted snapshot, including confirmed removals under D59. Correct through a new complete main capture. Existing-image changes need review; restoration may reuse exact eligible earlier acceptance under D35. D22 remains the separate Undo rule for saved human approval.

humanBaselineRejection.scope: Any current maintainer may reject a human-approved variant and atomically restore the prior baseline while its promotion is current. D24 protects automatically accepted variants; D22 remains the undo rule for a saved approval.

capturePreparation.scope: Ariakit prepares each page condition. The public adapter captures one variant per call and the reporter groups them by stable item key.
